description: Live view of what the market-data collectors are writing into the shared `dropset` database: candles, cross-source agreement, throughput, freshness, and coverage. Read top-down — the freshness tiles answer 'is ingestion alive right now', everything below answers 'and is it any good'.

panels.description:
The headline: the number the system believes, drawn over the prints it was built from. Three series per selected market — the composed fair price, the FX leg's fused estimate, and the FX leg's fast consensus median — against every selected source's raw ticks.

Read the GAPS, which is why all three are drawn rather than just the fair price. Fused-vs-fast is the estimator's whole contribution: they sit on top of each other while the sources agree, and separate exactly when one source is being ignored or a dislocation is being adopted. Fused-vs-scatter shows the estimator declining to chase a stray print. A fused line that tracks one source exclusively means the others are being trimmed or outweighed, which the weights panel below names.

The market and source pickers are INDEPENDENT and deliberately not auto-correlated: a market's symbol (EURC) and its FX product id (EUR-USD) are different vocabularies with no join in the schema, so pairing them is the operator's to do. Selecting a market whose sources are not also selected draws the fused line over an empty scatter, which is a picker mismatch and not a data gap.

targets.rawSql:
-- The estimator's output over its raw inputs. Each arm is a bare
-- column inside the epoch-filter macro: Grafana captures a macro
-- argument with a regex that stops at the first closing paren, so a
-- to_timestamp(...) call inside one truncates the argument and the
-- query fails to interpolate. The conversion happens in the SELECT
-- list, never in the macro.
--
-- Raw prints: the scatter the fused line is judged against.
SELECT
  to_timestamp(observed_at) AS "time",
  source || ' ' || product_id || ' tick' AS metric,
  price AS value
FROM spot_ticks
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(observed_at)
  AND source = ANY (ARRAY[${source:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[])
UNION ALL
-- The fair price: the composed mid the maker quotes off, which is now
-- built from the fused leg estimates rather than the bare medians.
-- NULL exactly when the composition paused, and left as a gap rather
-- than zero-filled -- a paused market and a market worth nothing are
-- different facts.
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  market || ' fair (fused)' AS metric,
  fair AS value
FROM maker_telemetry
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND market = ANY (ARRAY[${market:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND fair IS NOT NULL
UNION ALL
-- The FX leg's two numbers, which is where the estimator is actually
-- visible: `fused_value` is what the composition priced off and
-- `value` is the fast median that guards dislocations.
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  market || ' fx estimate (fused)' AS metric,
  fused_value AS value
FROM maker_legs
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND market = ANY (ARRAY[${market:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND leg = 'fx'
  AND fused_value IS NOT NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  market || ' fx consensus (fast)' AS metric,
  value
FROM maker_legs
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND market = ANY (ARRAY[${market:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND leg = 'fx'
ORDER BY 1

panels.title: Fair price over its sources

panels.description:
Each source's share of its leg's fused estimate, per tick. This is the panel that explains the one above: when the fused line stops tracking a source, this says by how much and from when.

A series pinned at ZERO is the interesting case, not an empty one. Zero means the source answered and was TRIMMED — it sat outside the dispersion band of the fast consensus, so the estimator declined to believe it. That is a sick feed, a mis-mapped product, or a genuine disagreement between an official reference rate and the tape, and it is exactly what must not be averaged away silently. A source that stopped answering has no row at all and leaves a gap instead.

Shares over one leg-tick sum to exactly 1 on a seeding or re-seeding tick -- trimming does not change that, because a trimmed source contributes no precision and so takes nothing out of the total. Only an ordinary update leaves them summing to less than 1, and that shortfall is the prior estimate's own share, deliberately not drawn because no feed is accountable for it.

targets.rawSql:
-- Per-source fusion weights. Deliberately NOT filtered to weight > 0:
-- a zero-weight row is a source that answered and was trimmed, which
-- is the single most useful thing this table records. Filtering it out
-- would leave a fused estimate with no record of what it refused.
--
-- The mechanism filter IS required, though, and for the opposite reason.
-- The table is keyed by mechanism so the resolver's consensus attribution
-- can land additively; those weights are exact linear-combination shares
-- rather than shares of posterior information. Omitting this predicate
-- would plot two vocabularies on one axis and double every series the
-- day they arrive.
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  market || ' ' || leg || ' ' || source AS metric,
  weight AS value
FROM maker_leg_contributions
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND mechanism = 'fusion'
  AND market = ANY (ARRAY[${market:sqlstring}]::text[])
ORDER BY 1

panels.title: Fusion weight by source

panels.description: Wall-clock seconds since each feed last committed a batch, straight off `feed_cursors.updated_at`. This is the only true wall-clock liveness signal in the schema — every other panel measures candle-bucket time, which a backfill can advance without the feed being currently healthy. A wall of green is the end-to-end proof that a feeds change works. Deliberately NOT filtered by the Source picker, unlike the candle-age tile beside it: feed_cursors is keyed by the framework's feed id (`cex:coinbase:EURC-USDC`), not by the `source` column, so the picker's values do not apply here.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  feed,
  extract(epoch FROM now() - updated_at) AS age_secs
FROM feed_cursors
ORDER BY feed

panels.title: Feed cursor age (wall clock)

panels.description: Seconds since the newest candle bucket each source/product has on record. The floor is one granularity by construction — the collector persists only closed buckets, so a perfectly healthy 60s feed reads 60-120s and never 0. The thresholds are set above that floor accordingly; treat this as 'how stale is the data I would quote from', and the cursor-age tile beside it as 'is the process alive'. The thresholds are absolute and calibrated for 60s buckets, which is the only granularity any collector writes today; selecting a coarser Granularity raises the floor above them and the tile reads permanently amber or red.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  source || ' ' || product_id AS feed,
  extract(epoch FROM now()) - max(bucket_start) AS age_secs
FROM cex_prices
WHERE source = ANY (ARRAY[${source:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND granularity_secs = ${granularity:sqlstring}::bigint
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1

panels.title: Last candle age

panels.description: OHLC candles as recorded, one panel per selected product. This is the 'real chart' view and the screenshot artifact. It reads a single source ($candle_source) on purpose: candles from two venues share a bucket key but are different series, so overlaying them would interleave bars rather than compare them. Use the overlay panel below to compare sources.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  to_timestamp(bucket_start) AS "time",
  "open",
  "high",
  "low",
  "close",
  "volume"
FROM cex_prices
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(bucket_start)
  AND source = ${candle_source:sqlstring}
  AND product_id = ${product_id:sqlstring}
  AND granularity_secs = ${granularity:sqlstring}::bigint
ORDER BY bucket_start

panels.title: OHLC $product_id ($candle_source, ${granularity}s buckets)

panels.description: Every selected source's closing print for every selected product, overlaid on one axis. Relative-value divergence is visible as separating lines: two venues quoting the same pair should track within basis, and a mispriced or mis-mapped source shows up on sight as a line at the wrong level. With one collector running this is a single series — it populates as sources land, with no dashboard edit.

targets.rawSql:
-- Candle closes and spot ticks in one series set. The tick half is
-- what makes this panel move BETWEEN candle closes: 60s is the finest
-- bucket any candle endpoint offers, so the candle half cannot show
-- intra-minute movement however often it is polled.
--
-- Tick series are suffixed so the legend distinguishes them from the
-- same venue's candle series, and they carry no granularity filter
-- because a tick has no bucket width.
SELECT
  to_timestamp(bucket_start) AS "time",
  source || ' ' || product_id AS metric,
  "close" AS value
FROM cex_prices
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(bucket_start)
  AND source = ANY (ARRAY[${source:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND granularity_secs = ${granularity:sqlstring}::bigint
UNION ALL
SELECT
  to_timestamp(observed_at) AS "time",
  source || ' ' || product_id || ' tick' AS metric,
  price AS value
FROM spot_ticks
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(observed_at)
  AND source = ANY (ARRAY[${source:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[])
ORDER BY 1

panels.title: Price by source

panels.description: Rows landed per minute, per source. Note the axis is candle-bucket time, not insert time: the schema records no insert timestamp, so this counts buckets by the minute they cover. For a live 60s feed that is a flat line at one row per product per minute, and a collector that dies mid-window drops visibly to zero. A collector dead for the whole window contributes no series at all rather than a zero line - that case is what the freshness tiles above are for. The bucket is a fixed one minute rather than the dashboard interval, so the number means the same thing at every zoom level; the cost is that a multi-day range returns a point per minute.

targets.rawSql:
-- The CTE is load-bearing, not style. Grafana captures macro
-- arguments with a regex that stops at the first closing paren, so
-- wrapping the epoch column in a to_timestamp call inside the
-- time-group macro leaves it one truncated argument and the query
-- fails to interpolate. Converting the column in a CTE first hands
-- the macro a bare column name, which is all it can parse. For the
-- same reason, do not name a macro in a comment here: the scanner
-- does not skip comments and will try to interpolate the example.
WITH bucketed AS (
  SELECT
    to_timestamp(bucket_start) AS bucket_ts,
    source
  FROM cex_prices
  WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(bucket_start)
    AND source = ANY (ARRAY[${source:sqlstring}]::text[])
    AND product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[])
    AND granularity_secs = ${granularity:sqlstring}::bigint
)
SELECT
  $__timeGroupAlias(bucket_ts, '1m', 0),
  source AS metric,
  count(*) AS value
FROM bucketed
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1

panels.title: Candle rows per minute by source

panels.description: Which source covers which product, over the last $coverage_mins minutes. This is the panel that answers 'do we want another collector here' - a product with one source has no cross-check, and a product with none is a gap. Deliberately NOT filtered by the source/product variables: its job is to show everything arriving, including series the current selection hides.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  source,
  product_id,
  granularity_secs,
  count(*) AS buckets,
  to_timestamp(max(bucket_start)) AS latest_bucket,
  (extract(epoch FROM now()) - max(bucket_start))::bigint AS age_secs
FROM cex_prices
WHERE bucket_start >= extract(epoch FROM now()) - (${coverage_mins:sqlstring}::bigint * 60)
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3

panels.title: Candle coverage (last $coverage_mins min)

panels.description: The same question as the candle coverage panel above, for the tick tier - which venues are printing which products into spot_ticks. Separate rather than merged into that panel because the two tiers have genuinely different columns: a candle row has a bucket width and OHLCV, a tick row has neither. Watch the confidence column: a venue that publishes one (Pyth) and suddenly stops is a different event from one that never had a confidence notion at all, which is why it is a count rather than a flag. Deliberately NOT filtered by the source/product variables, for the same reason as the panel above.

targets.rawSql:
-- Age thresholds are tighter than the candle panel's on purpose: a tick
-- feed polling every 15s that has printed nothing for a minute is behind
-- in a way a 60s candle series would not be.
SELECT
  source,
  product_id,
  count(*) AS prints,
  count(confidence) AS with_confidence,
  to_timestamp(max(observed_at)) AS latest_print,
  (extract(epoch FROM now()) - max(observed_at))::bigint AS age_secs
FROM spot_ticks
WHERE observed_at >= extract(epoch FROM now()) - (${coverage_mins:sqlstring}::bigint * 60)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2

panels.title: Tick coverage (last $coverage_mins min)

panels.description: Every source the collectors registered, contributing or not - the completeness guarantee the two panels above cannot give. Both of those group over a measurement table, so a source that wrote nothing has no rows to group and is simply absent, which on a panel is indistinguishable from never having been configured. This one drives from instrument_registry instead, so a dark collector is a row reading 0 that sorts to the top. Read it when the question is 'is this source contributing anywhere' - Pyth included, whose ticks reach only the panel above and only while it is actually printing. Three columns, and the distinction between them is the point: 'products' is what the collector registered, 'ever_produced' how many of those have ever written a row, and 'live' how many are inside their staleness bound. ever_produced = 0 is a collector that has never worked; ever_produced = products with live = 0 is one that worked and died, and 'latest' says when. live < products is a partial outage. The bound is class-aware rather than a fixed window, so a daily-cadence source is not reported dead every load and an FX pair clears its weekend. TWO THINGS TO KNOW BEFORE TREATING A DARK ROW AS A FAULT. First, a source may be deliberately PARKED - pyth is, pending a credential, so it reads ever_produced=27 live=0 indefinitely and that is correct; expected-dark sources are recorded on their Linear issue, and any OTHER dark source is a fault. Second, the bars leg measures bucket_start, not write time, so a daily source is already ~1-2 days stale while healthy; across a weekend that can reach the 72h fx-pair bound and read quiet on a Monday. This panel reads its verdict from instrument_source_liveness rather than computing one, so widening for the daily case is a change to that view and every consumer follows it at once - which is exactly why the bounds are not restated here. Deliberately NOT filtered by the Source or Product variables: a panel answering 'what is missing' must not be narrowed by a picker populated from the same registry.

targets.rawSql:
-- Every source the collectors REGISTERED, whether or not it is producing.
-- The two coverage panels above group over a measurement table, so a source
-- that wrote nothing in the window has no rows to group and vanishes
-- entirely; absence there cannot be told apart from never having been
-- configured. Driving from the registry inverts that, and a dark collector
-- becomes a row reading 0 rather than a row that is not there.
--
-- PER (SOURCE, PRODUCT), NOT PER PRODUCT, and that is the whole point.
-- instrument_liveness answers the same question one level up and
-- deliberately drops the source, so a product some OTHER collector still
-- covers reads live and the dead one is masked. That masking is exactly the
-- defect this panel exists to catch, and instrument_source_liveness is the
-- view that keeps the source.
--
-- READ FROM THE VIEW, do not recompute. This panel first carried its own
-- copy of the two class-aware staleness bounds, because no per-source view
-- existed when it was written. One does now, and it defines those constants
-- once — so a copy here could only drift from them, and the whole reason the
-- thresholds live in one place is that a silent divergence between two
-- liveness verdicts is indistinguishable from a real outage. The view also
-- carries the granularity-vocabulary constraint that keeps the bars lookup
-- an index seek rather than a range scan, which this panel needs on a 5s
-- refresh and now inherits rather than restates.
SELECT
  source,
  count(*) AS products,
  count(last_data_at) AS ever_produced,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_live) AS live,
  to_timestamp(max(last_data_at)) AS latest,
  (extract(epoch FROM now()) - max(last_data_at))::bigint AS age_secs
FROM instrument_source_liveness
GROUP BY source
ORDER BY live ASC, source ASC

panels.title: Source coverage (registry-driven)

panels.description: The quoting criterion, shown directly rather than by implication: per pair, is a trusted tape live, and how much margin stands behind it. Read 'trusted_live' and nothing else to answer go or no-go - it is the only column colored, because it is the only one that decides anything. 0 means this pair cannot be quoted and the maker halts on it; 1 means it can. THE CRITERION IS ONE LIVE TRUSTED TAPE, halt at zero, ruled by the operator on 2026-09-10. It replaced a 'survives one or two venues dark' reading that no panel could implement, because it also asserted that two intraday sources satisfied it and two sources with two dark leaves none. The trusted tape is oanda, by designation rather than by measurement - it is the anchor treated as truth. Twelve Data carries the same pairs and is deliberately not believable alone, which is why the two are never pooled into one count: one-live-of-two tells you nothing until you know which one it was. 'margin_sources' is every other source that is live and fresh - context, not a requirement, and it cannot clear the halt. One honest edge shown rather than hidden: a daily source counts toward 'margin_sources' for the freshness window after it publishes, which is harmless precisely because margin decides nothing and a daily reference can never reach 'trusted_live'. 'live_but_stale' is where an outage lands FIRST, and note it is a TRANSITION bucket rather than a cumulative one: past the class staleness bound the source moves on into 'dark', so this counter rises and then falls back to zero rather than climbing with the outage. Past that point the red 'trusted_live' is the only trace, which is sufficient for go/no-go but will not tell you a long-dead source from one never rostered. Daily sources also sit in 'live_but_stale' between publications, so read it against 'fresh_sources' to tell an outage from a cadence. 'dark' is registered and outside its class staleness bound, and is deliberately NOT color-coded: it pools a parked source with a faulted one, and Pyth is parked pending a credential, so every row reads dark=1 today - coloring that red on every row is the train-the-operator-to-ignore-red failure that keeping parked quiet exists to prevent. Until parked and faulted render distinctly, this column is a constant and carries no information. The three MVP anchors sort first and are always present even if de-rostered, so an anchor no collector registers is a row of zeros rather than a missing row - including dark=0, because that column counts REGISTERED sources and there are none. Deliberately not called a 'dark anchor': that state is caught by trusted_live going red, not by the dark column, which reads 0 there and 1 in today's benign parked-Pyth state. Deliberately NOT filtered by the Source or Product pickers, for the same reason Source coverage is not: a panel answering 'what is thin' must not be narrowed by a picker.

targets.rawSql:
-- Live venues per pair: the quoting criterion, shown directly rather than by
-- implication.
--
-- THE CRITERION IS ONE LIVE TRUSTED TAPE, halt at zero -- ruled by the
-- operator on 2026-09-10, replacing a "survives one or two venues dark"
-- reading that could not be implemented because it contradicted itself. So
-- trusted_live is the only column that decides anything, and it is the only
-- one colored. Everything beside it is context: margin_sources is what stands
-- behind the tape, not a second requirement.
--
-- The trusted tape is oanda, named here as a literal because primacy is a
-- DESIGNATION rather than a measurement -- it is the anchor treated as truth,
-- and no column in the store records that. Twelve Data carries the same pairs
-- intraday and is deliberately not believable alone, which is precisely why
-- the two must not be pooled into one count: one-live-of-two says nothing
-- until you know which one.
--
-- WHY THERE IS NO CADENCE CLASSIFIER HERE, since the obvious way to write
-- this panel has one and it is a trap. An earlier version split sources into
-- intraday and daily by counting readings in a six-hour window, which fails
-- in the worst possible direction: a genuinely intraday venue that has been
-- down for more than six hours has no readings in the window, so it stops
-- counting as intraday and lands in the daily population -- while
-- instrument_source_liveness still reports it live, because that bound is 48
-- to 72 hours. A long outage therefore made the panel look HEALTHIER, moving
-- a failed venue into a bucket that is supposed to look old. Verified against
-- the store: a source can be is_live with zero readings in six hours.
--
-- Freshness alone does the work instead, and under the ruled criterion that
-- is sufficient rather than a compromise: cadence only ever mattered as a
-- proxy for "could this price a quote right now", and a designated tape plus
-- a recency test answers that directly. It is also fail-closed, which the
-- classifier was not -- when the tape stops printing, trusted_live goes to
-- zero and stays there.
--
-- One honest edge, visible rather than hidden: a daily source counts toward
-- margin_sources for the freshness window after it publishes. That is why
-- margin_sources is context and not a criterion. It can never reach
-- trusted_live, so it cannot clear the halt -- which is exactly what the
-- ruling requires of a daily reference.
--
-- THE MVP ANCHORS ARE A LITERAL, which is deliberate and not an oversight.
-- There is no legitimate state in which an MVP anchor is absent, so this
-- panel has to be unable to lose one. A de-rostered product leaves the
-- registry, so a purely registry-driven read would drop it silently -- the
-- same invisible-rather-than-dark defect one level up that the coverage panel
-- exists to catch. Naming the three keeps a dark anchor rendering as a row of
-- zeros. They order first and are not otherwise displayed: the row order
-- already says it, so a column restating it would be sort machinery on show.
WITH anchor AS (
  SELECT a.product_id
  FROM (VALUES
    ('EUR-USD'),
    ('AUD-USD'),
    ('CAD-USD')
  ) AS a (product_id)
),

scope AS (
  SELECT a.product_id FROM anchor AS a
  UNION
  SELECT l.product_id FROM instrument_source_liveness AS l
),

graded AS (
  SELECT
    s.product_id,
    l.source,
    l.is_live,
    -- Read the liveness verdict from the view and the recency test here. The
    -- two answer different questions: is_live is "should this source be
    -- producing at all", on a class-aware bound that tolerates an FX weekend,
    -- while fresh is "is it producing right now".
    extract(epoch FROM now()) - l.last_data_at
      <= ${quote_freshness_mins:sqlstring}::bigint * 60 AS fresh,
    -- COUPLED to the exact source spelling the collectors register. The feeds
    -- framework names some sources per product (a venue can register as
    -- `venue:PRODUCT`), so if oanda ever adopted that shape this equality
    -- would stop matching and every pair would read trusted_live = 0. That
    -- fails CLOSED -- a permanent false halt, loud rather than silent, and
    -- diagnosable because the venue still appears in fresh_sources -- which is
    -- why it is left as a plain equality rather than a prefix match that could
    -- also match a different venue whose name merely starts the same way.
    l.source = 'oanda' AS trusted
  FROM scope AS s
  LEFT JOIN instrument_source_liveness AS l ON l.product_id = s.product_id
)

SELECT
  g.product_id,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE g.is_live AND g.trusted AND g.fresh) AS trusted_live,
  count(*) FILTER (
    WHERE g.is_live AND NOT g.trusted AND g.fresh
  ) AS margin_sources,
  -- Where an outage lands FIRST, which is not where it stays: past the class
  -- bound the source moves on into dark, so this counter rises and then falls
  -- back to zero. It is a TRANSITION bucket, not a cumulative one, and saying
  -- otherwise would be the same kind of overstatement as the cadence classifier
  -- above. A daily source also sits here between publications, so read it
  -- against fresh_sources to tell an outage from a cadence.
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE g.is_live AND NOT g.fresh) AS live_but_stale,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT g.is_live) AS dark,
  string_agg(g.source, ', ' ORDER BY g.source) FILTER (
    WHERE g.is_live AND g.fresh
  ) AS fresh_sources
FROM graded AS g
GROUP BY g.product_id
ORDER BY
  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM anchor AS a WHERE a.product_id = g.product_id) DESC,
  trusted_live ASC,
  g.product_id ASC

panels.title: Live venues per pair

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT asset_class FROM instruments ORDER BY 1
list.description: Asset class, from the instruments dimension - the class a pair's two legs imply rather than a label anyone maintains, so re-seeding a currency's kind reclassifies every pair using it with nothing to backfill. Queried rather than hardcoded for the same reason the Product picker is: a fixed list is wrong the moment the roster changes, and wrong silently. Expect an 'unclassified' bucket to be selectable - the dimension left-joins deliberately so a pair whose leg is not yet seeded stays visible rather than vanishing from every class filter, which would hide its data while the panel still rendered.
list.label: Class
list.name: class
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT asset_class FROM instruments ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT product_id FROM instruments WHERE asset_class = ANY (ARRAY[${class:sqlstring}]::text[]) ORDER BY 1
list.description: Every product any collector is configured to poll, from the instruments dimension, narrowed to the selected Class. Registry-driven rather than a scan of the measurement tables, which matters three ways: it covers both tiers by construction - most of the roster is tick-only, since only EURC reaches a CEX candle endpoint - a newly added pair appears before its first row lands, and it costs one small-table read instead of a DISTINCT over two unbounded tables on every dashboard load. The class filter uses the sqlstring formatter inside an ARRAY, not a regex inside a quoted literal: the regex formatter does not escape quotes, and ARRAY[] stays valid SQL when nothing is selected where IN () is a syntax error. Defaults to the three MVP FX pairs rather than All, and that default is load-bearing rather than taste: the OHLC panel repeats over this variable at full width, so All renders one full-width chart per instrument. At 33 instruments that is 33 stacked charts pushing roughly 330 grid rows between the top of the dashboard and everything under it - including Tick coverage and Source coverage, which are the only two panels where a tick-only venue such as Kraken appears at all. Most of those charts are also empty, since the default candle source carries candles for a single product. Drill-down is unaffected: the drop-down still offers every product and All.
list.label: Product
list.name: product_id
list.query: SELECT product_id FROM instruments WHERE asset_class = ANY (ARRAY[${class:sqlstring}]::text[]) ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM instrument_registry ORDER BY 1
list.description: Sources from both tiers, so the tick-only venues (kraken, pyth, erapi, frankfurter) are selectable rather than absent. Note that 'coinbase' appears once but writes both tiers - the table a row lives in is what distinguishes a print from a bucket, not the source label.
list.label: Source
list.name: source
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM instrument_registry ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT market FROM maker_legs ORDER BY 1
list.description: Markets the maker has written a leg row for. A separate vocabulary from the Product picker and not joinable to it: a market is keyed by its token symbol (EURC) while a feed product is a pair id (EUR-USD), and the schema holds no mapping between them. Empty on a database no maker has run against, which blanks the two fused panels and leaves the ingestion panels below unaffected - the collectors and the maker are independent writers.
list.label: Market
list.name: market
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT market FROM maker_legs ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM cex_prices ORDER BY 1
list.description: The single source the candlestick panel draws. Candles from two venues cannot share one set of bars. This default is paired with the Product default and must stay paired: the panel filters on BOTH, so a source that carries none of the defaulted products paints nothing at all. oanda carries EUR-USD and AUD-USD, two of the three MVP anchors, so the panel paints on first load; coinbase, the previous default, carries candles for EURC-USDC alone and would leave every repeat empty. CAD-USD renders empty against any source until it joins the keyed venues' roster, and that emptiness is a true signal rather than a fault.
list.label: Candle source
list.name: candle_source
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM cex_prices ORDER BY 1

list.description: Bucket size to chart, in seconds. A fixed list rather than a query on the data, so it is never empty on a cold database - an empty value would make every query that filters on it a syntax error instead of a 'no data' panel. 60 is the collector's GRANULARITY_SECS default, and today the only value any collector writes — selecting a coarser one blanks every panel until some collector is configured to record it.

list.description: How recent a source's newest reading must be to count as printing right now, on the redundancy panel. This is that panel's whole liveness test: it decides trusted_live, margin_sources and live_but_stale between them, and there is deliberately no cadence classifier beside it - an earlier version had one and it failed open, reclassifying a long-dead intraday venue as a daily source. TREAT THIS AS THE HALT'S DETECTION LATENCY, not as a display preference: it is how long the tape may go quiet before the pair reads no-go, so 15 and 360 differ by nearly six hours of blindness. The default of 15 is not arbitrary - it mirrors the maker's own per-leg tape staleness bound, so the panel goes red no later than the engine refuses the leg. A looser setting opens a window in which the maker would reject the tape while this panel still reads green, which is why the list reaches below the default rather than starting at it. The one thing no setting can do is let a daily reference clear the halt, since only the designated tape reaches trusted_live. URL sync is deliberately OFF, unlike the other variables here, and the reason is an asymmetry rather than any envelope the option list provides: a picker value is CHOSEN and stays visible in the picker, while a URL value is ADOPTED SILENTLY from a shared or stale link. The list is explicitly not a safe bound - 1440 is 96x the maker's tape bound and would let a day-dead tape read live, which is why it is offered for reading history rather than for watching a live position. What makes that acceptable from the picker and not from a link is that choosing it is a decision somebody made and can still see. A fixed list rather than a query, so it can never be empty and make every filter that reads it a syntax error.
list.label: Minimum quotable freshness (min)
list.name: quote_freshness_mins
